references.text: Rules for priests regarding who they could approach when someone was dead. The priest in the parable may have avoided the injured man out of fear of becoming ceremonially unclean, which relates to the priests' purity regulations in Leviticus.

Regulations concerning uncleanness from touching a dead body. The priest in the parable may have assumed the man was dead and wished to avoid ritual impurity, which would have prevented him from serving.
Hosea quotes God's words: 'For I desire mercy, not sacrifice.' The priest prioritized ritual purity over mercy, contrary to God's true will.
'To do justice and righteousness is more valuable to the Lord than sacrifice.' The priest neglected justice and mercy in favor of external religious duty.
The next verse tells that a Levite also passed by the injured man, reinforcing the point that religious leaders failed in showing mercy.
In contrast to the priest, the Samaritan man showed mercy, which is the main point of Jesus' parable—true neighborly love surpasses religious status.
James writes that faith without works is dead—to see a brother in need and merely pass by without helping is meaningless, just like the priest who passed by the injured man.
John writes: 'If anyone has material possessions and sees a brother or sister in need but has no pity on them, how can the love of God be in that person?' This parallels the priest's action.
Micah summarizes what the Lord requires: to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God—the opposite of the priest's behavior in the parable.
Ezekiel speaks against shepherds (leaders) in Israel who do not care for the weak, sick, and injured. The priest in the parable represents such a neglectful leader.
